metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the participant's choice aligns with the strict prediction of the Tallying heuristic, computed only on trials where Tallying has a strict preference (i.e., one option has more winning features than the other). The experimental design includes multiple trials where Tallying and WADD make diametrically opposed predictions (e.g., Tallying favors the option with many weak features, while WADD favors the option with fewer strong features). Consequently, data generated by the Tallying model will yield a high score on this metric, whereas data generated by the WADD model will yield a score significantly below 0.5.

Focuses exclusively on Trial 1, the most discriminative trial type in the design. On this trial, one option has 2 high-validity features (favored by WADD) while the other has 3 low-validity features (favored by Tallying). The metric computes the proportion of choices for the Tallying-favored option. Tallying will yield a high value (close to 1), while WADD will yield a low value (close to 0).

The experimental design constructs 5 specific trial types where the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic and the Weighted Additive (WADD) rule make strictly opposing predictions. TTB always chooses the option favored by the single highest-validity discriminating feature, whereas WADD integrates all features and is designed to choose the opposite option because the sum of lower-validity features outweighs the single best feature. By calculating the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the TTB prediction, we can perfectly discriminate the two models. TTB will score close to 1.0 (subject to noise), while WADD will score close to 0.0.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that are consistent with a baseline Weighted Additive (WADD) model that directly uses the feature validities as weights. The experimental trials are specifically designed to pit the highest-validity feature (which Take-The-Best relies on) against the combined weight of several lower-validity features. Thus, the TTB model will systematically make choices opposite to this baseline WADD prediction, resulting in a score near 0 (modulo noise), whereas the advocated WADD model will produce a high consistency score.

This metric calculates the difference in the probability of choosing Option A between Trial 2 (A=[1,0,0,0,0], B=[0,0,0,0,0]) and Trial 5 (A=[1,0,0,0,0], B=[0,1,1,1,0]). Under Take The Best (TTB), the first discriminating feature in both trials is the first feature, which favors A. Thus, TTB predicts an identical core preference for A in both trials, meaning the difference in choice rates will be near 0 on average, regardless of the subject's noise level. Under Bounded Sequential Feature Sampling (BSFS), subjects with a threshold of 2 or 3 will choose A in Trial 2 but will accumulate enough opposing evidence from the subsequent features to choose B in Trial 5. This results in a large positive difference (~1.0 for those subjects), creating a substantial mean gap between the theories that easily achieves statistical significance.

In this experimental design, Take The Best (TTB) evaluates the first feature and immediately chooses Option A in almost all trials. Bounded Sequential Feature Sampling (BSFS) with a threshold > 1 will continue sampling and often choose Option B due to the strong opposing evidence in the remaining features. Calculating the mean response (proportion of B choices) will yield a value near 0 for TTB and a significantly higher value for BSFS.
